title: Summary, note, table and flow-chart completion

guide.p: Completion tasks give you a summary, notes, a table or a flow-chart with gaps. The answers are words taken directly from the passage (or letters from a word list). They test whether you can locate specific information and fit it into a paraphrased context.

bullets: Words from the passage: copy the words exactly, with the same spelling. Do not change the form of the word.
Word list (A, B, C…): write the letter. The list contains synonyms of words in the passage, so you need to understand the meaning, not just match words.
Read the title of the summary, table or flow-chart — it often tells you which paragraphs to look at.
Predict the type of word for each gap: noun, verb, adjective, number, singular or plural.
Answers usually follow passage order in summaries and flow-charts. Tables may be read across or down.
Find the matching section, then find the exact word that fits both meaning and grammar.
Check the word limit and spelling. A number written as digits counts as one number.

guide.tip: Flow-charts describe a process. Look for sequence words in the passage: first, then, next, after this, finally.

paragraphs.text: Paper is one of the most widely recycled materials, yet few people know what happens after a newspaper goes into the recycling bin. The process takes place in a factory called a paper mill, in a series of stages, each designed to remove something that would spoil the finished product.

First, the collected paper is sorted by grade, because office paper, cardboard and newspaper contain fibres of different quality. The sorted paper is then mixed with water and chemicals in a large machine called a pulper, which breaks it down into a wet mixture of fibres known as pulp.

Next, the pulp is forced through screens with small holes to remove staples, plastic and glue. It is then spun in cone-shaped cleaners, where heavier particles such as sand are thrown outwards and removed. To remove printing ink, air is bubbled through the pulp; the ink sticks to the bubbles and rises to the surface as foam, which is skimmed off. If white paper is required, the pulp may also be bleached.

Finally, the clean pulp is sprayed onto a moving wire mesh, where water drains away and the fibres bond together into a sheet. Heated rollers then press and dry the sheet before it is wound into enormous rolls.

Unfortunately, paper fibres cannot be recycled for ever. Each time they are processed they become shorter and weaker, and after five to seven cycles they are too short to form a sheet. For this reason, some new wood fibre is usually added to keep recycled paper strong.
